package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered as standalone JavaScript files, not via a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple unique samples, see SHA256 IOCs)
package_info.why_malicious: The JavaScript files are designed to impersonate legitimate Windows Security updates, but instead execute fileless malware in memory, bypass user access controls, delete system backups, and ultimately deliver and execute Magniber ransomware, resulting in data encryption and extortion.

execution_context.trigger: user-execution (when user opens the fake update JavaScript file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user execution, the JavaScript spawns a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, which loads and executes additional malicious payloads directly in memory, enabling fileless infection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate update scripts should not spawn hidden PowerShell processes or bypass execution policies. This behavior is typical of malware loaders.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal update scripts would use official update mechanisms and not require direct PowerShell execution or memory-only payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise deployment scripts may use PowerShell for automation, but not in the context of user-facing update prompts.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after PowerShell is launched by JavaScript)
execution_context.file_location: In-memory PowerShell payload (never written to disk)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
# Pseudocode representation
powershell.exe -Command "vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet; wbadmin delete catalog -quiet; bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No; bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell payload deletes all shadow copies and disables Windows backup and recovery features, preventing the victim from restoring their files after encryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting shadow copies and disabling recovery is a classic ransomware tactic to prevent data recovery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate update scripts should never interfere with system backups or recovery settings.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, IT administrators may use these commands for system maintenance, but never in user-initiated update scripts.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after backup deletion, before/while ransomware payload is loaded)
execution_context.file_location: In-memory PowerShell or shellcode (never written to disk)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell downloads and executes the Magniber ransomware payload directly in memory, often using syscalls to avoid user-mode API hooks, resulting in file encryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing code from an untrusted remote server is a hallmark of malware. Use of syscalls to evade detection is highly advanced and malicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should never download and execute code from untrusted sources, especially not in memory.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may download signed updates, but never execute them in this manner.

attack_chain.action: User is tricked into downloading and executing a JavaScript file masquerading as a Windows Security update.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial code execution and PowerShell payload launch

attack_chain.action: JavaScript spawns a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, loading the next stage in memory.
PowerShell payload deletes shadow copies and disables backup/recovery features to prevent data restoration.
attack_chain.leads_to: System is left without backup or recovery options

attack_chain.action: PowerShell downloads and executes the Magniber ransomware payload directly in memory, often using syscalls to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware encrypts user files and displays ransom note

behavioral_signatures: User-initiated execution of JavaScript files outside browser context
JavaScript spawning hidden PowerShell processes with execution policy bypass
PowerShell deleting shadow copies and disabling recovery features
In-memory code execution and use of syscalls to evade user-mode hooks
file_indicators: Unexpected .js files named like Windows updates (e.g., 'Windows.Security.Update.js')
No persistent malware files on disk (fileless execution)
Absence of shadow copies and backup catalogs after suspicious activity
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to known Magniber domains (e.g., totwo[.]pw, ittakes[.]fun, catat[.]site, etc.)
PowerShell or JavaScript making web requests to untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for user-initiated execution of JavaScript files outside of browsers, especially those that spawn PowerShell with execution policy bypassed and hidden windows. Alert on PowerShell commands that delete shadow copies or disable recovery features. Detect in-memory-only malware activity and outbound connections to known Magniber domains. Correlate the absence of backup/restore points with suspicious script execution.
